headline: Dutch Startup Grows Moss on City Walls to Cool and Green Urban Spaces
meta_description: Respyre's Mosscrete coating lets moss grow on building facades without soil or irrigation, tested across eight projects in Belgium and the Netherlands.
summary_short: A Dutch company has developed a coating that lets moss grow directly on concrete, requiring only rain and air—no maintenance needed.
body:
What if buildings could slowly come alive? A Dutch startup called Respyre has developed Mosscrete, a bioreceptive concrete coating that allows moss to grow directly on vertical surfaces using only moisture from rain and air. Based on research from Delft University of Technology, the technology has already been applied across eight real-world projects in Belgium and the Netherlands, from industrial warehouses to noise barriers and social housing. Unlike traditional green walls, which demand soil, structural support, irrigation systems, and regular maintenance, Mosscrete works as a simple coating applied to existing or new facades. Moss attaches through rhizoids—tiny thread-like structures that cling without damaging the material underneath.

The eight test sites reveal how versatile the approach can be. A 450-square-meter warehouse facade in Kortrijk, Belgium, was integrated with rainwater harvesting for a completely maintenance-free system. In Hoofddorp, the Netherlands, a 300-square-meter noise barrier is being tested with passive greening, relying on natural moisture alone. A social housing project in Purmerend proved the technology was more affordable than traditional greening options, while a commercial renovation in Haarlem combined Mosscrete with insulation to explore whether moss could improve thermal performance—research published in June 2026 found that wet moss creates cooling through evaporation, though dry moss can overheat.

What makes Mosscrete genuinely different is its philosophy. Most building materials are engineered to resist change, staying sealed and gray for decades. Respyre designed this coating for the opposite: to welcome transformation. As moss gradually colonizes a wall, it helps cities manage stormwater and heat while supporting local biodiversity. A moss-covered building doesn't look neglected—it looks alive.
